clinician.trajectory_summary: A 31-year-old Caucasian female smoker presented with a 7-week history of fever, night sweats, joint pains, myalgia, and nasal congestion. She had been hospitalized 3 weeks prior for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with left lower lobe consolidation on CT. On readmission, despite antibiotic therapy, fever persisted and new symptoms emerged: dizziness, hearing impairment, conjunctival injection with episcleritis, maculopapular rash over upper limbs, and nodular tender lesions over lower limbs. Audiometry confirmed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Skin biopsy of the lower limb lesions demonstrated small and medium-sized vessel vasculitis with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Comprehensive serologic testing (ANA, ANCA, ASMA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, complement levels) was negative, excluding other vasculitides and supporting the seronegative nature of Cogan's syndrome. Inflammatory markers (CRP and WCC) were elevated and responded to steroid therapy. The clinical presentation fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for Cogan's syndrome: the classic triad of audiovestibular involvement (bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and dizziness), ocular inflammation (episcleritis with conjunctival injection), and systemic vasculitis (confirmed histopathologically).

On readmission, despite antibiotic therapy, fever persisted and new symptoms emerged: dizziness, hearing impairment, conjunctival injection with episcleritis, maculopapular rash over upper limbs, and nodular tender lesions over lower limbs. Audiometry confirmed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Skin biopsy of the lower limb lesions demonstrated small and medium-sized vessel vasculitis with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Comprehensive serologic testing (ANA, ANCA, ASMA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, complement levels) was negative, excluding other vasculitides and supporting the seronegative nature of Cogan's syndrome. Inflammatory markers (CRP and WCC) were elevated and responded to steroid therapy. The clinical presentation fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for Cogan's syndrome: the classic triad of audiovestibular involvement (bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and dizziness), ocular inflammation (episcleritis with conjunctival injection), and systemic vasculitis (confirmed histopathologically).
